stem: Karrabee Cove Hotels, a Phillip Island company with 400 staff that runs six hotels, is setting its priorities for next year. Which statement is an objective rather than a goal?
options: Make every guest's stay comfortable, welcoming and worth repeating
Improve the security of the guest data held in company systems
Cut the average time to confirm a booking to under three minutes by 30 June
Give guests a better and simpler online experience when booking rooms
explanation: Only this statement sets a measurable target (under three minutes) and a deadline (30 June), so Karrabee Cove Hotels can check whether it has been met. The others are broad aims.
whyWrong: A broad aim with no measure or deadline, so it is a goal.
It names an area to improve but gives no measure or deadline, so it is a goal.
'Better' and 'simpler' can't be measured as written, and there is no deadline, so it is a goal.

stem: Sallygum Health, a network of Bendigo medical clinics with 600 staff, has the goal of improving patients' access to care. Which proposed software project most directly supports this goal?
options: An online booking app that lets patients book and change appointments at any hour
A payroll module that calculates staff overtime and leave balances automatically
An internal wiki where the clinics' developers record their coding standards
A stock control program that reorders medical supplies when levels run low
explanation: Letting patients book and change appointments at any time removes a barrier to seeing a clinician, so this project serves the access goal directly.
whyWrong: It makes administration more efficient but doesn't change how patients reach care.
It supports the development team's consistency, not patients' access to care.
It keeps the clinics supplied, but it doesn't make appointments easier to get.

stem: Karrabee Cove Hotels has the goal of reducing its environmental impact. Which objective best supports this goal?
options: Use the new energy-management software to make every hotel more environmentally friendly
Increase revenue from winter bookings by 15% within the next 18 months
Move the booking system to a cloud-based platform by the end of the financial year
Reduce the electricity used per occupied room by 10% within 18 months
explanation: It is measurable (10% less electricity per occupied room), has a time frame (18 months) and relates directly to environmental impact, so progress towards the goal can be checked.
whyWrong: It relates to the goal but has no measure or time frame, so it reads as another goal.
It is measurable, but it serves a financial goal, and more guests could increase the company's impact.
It has a deadline, but nothing in it measures environmental impact.

stem: Yellowbox Credit Union, a Ballarat lender with 250 staff, has the goal of keeping its members' trust. One objective is that no member data is exposed through its software over the next two years. Its developers currently test new features using a copy of real member records. Which change best serves this objective?
options: Rewrite the objective as 'improve data security' so that it covers every department
Test new features with realistic invented records instead of copies of real member data
Require internal documentation in every module that reads or writes member records
Give all staff access to the test environment so that faults are reported sooner
explanation: Real member records in a test environment can be seen by anyone with test access, or leaked in a breach of that environment. Invented records remove this exposure while still allowing thorough testing.
whyWrong: This turns a measurable objective into a vague goal and does nothing to reduce exposure.
Documentation helps maintenance but doesn't stop real records being exposed during testing.
Wider access to a test environment holding real data increases the chance of exposure.

stem: Budgeree Hills Community Health, a network of Gippsland clinics with 450 staff, has launched a program that sends each patient an SMS reminder two days before their appointment. Its objective is that no more than 8% of bookings are missed in the first 12 months after launch, down from 12% in the year before. Which data would best show whether this objective has been met?
options: The number of reminder messages the program sent in the 12 months after launch
Missed appointments as a percentage of bookings in the 12 months after launch
Patients' ratings of the reminder messages in a survey run six months after launch
The total number of appointments missed in the 12 months after the launch
explanation: The objective is stated as a percentage of bookings over the first 12 months after launch, so the data must give that same measure for that same period. Comparing it with the 8% target shows whether the objective was met.
whyWrong: Messages sent measure the program's activity, not whether fewer appointments were missed.
Ratings show how patients feel about the messages, not how many appointments were missed.
A count can't be checked against a percentage target: if bookings grew, the count could rise while the rate fell.

stem: Saltgrass Flat Energy, an electricity retailer in Morwell with 700 staff, has the goal of being the energy retailer its customers trust most. One objective is to launch a new billing app by 1 March. Three weeks before that date, the project manager proposes skipping code reviews so that the launch date can be met. Which response best serves the company's goal?
options: Skip the reviews, because the launch date can be measured and customer trust can't
Skip the reviews for now, then review all of the code in one batch after the launch
Review only the code that junior developers have written in the last three weeks
Keep the reviews and move the date or cut features, since flaws could cost trust
explanation: An objective exists to serve a goal. Launching on time with unreviewed code risks releasing security flaws in an app that handles customers' billing details, and a breach would work directly against the goal of being the most trusted retailer. Moving the date or launching with fewer features keeps the reviews in place.
whyWrong: Being measurable doesn't make the objective more important than the goal it is meant to serve.
Any flaws would be live, with customers' billing data exposed, until the batch review found them.
Experienced developers make mistakes too, so unreviewed code could still contain vulnerabilities.

stem: Treecreeper Mutual, a Warrnambool insurer with 1100 staff, has the goal of improving its customer service. Its objective was to answer 85% of phone calls within three minutes by 30 June. New call-routing software met this target in May, but over the same months, complaints about being transferred between departments doubled. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The objective was met, but it may not be moving the insurer towards its goal
The goal has been achieved, because its objective was met before the deadline
The objective has not been met, because customers are still making complaints
The software has failed, so the insurer should return to its old phone system
explanation: The target was measured and reached, so the objective was met. But an objective is only useful as evidence of progress towards the goal, and doubled complaints suggest customer service may not have improved. Treecreeper Mutual should review whether its objectives measure what the goal needs, for example by adding one about calls resolved without a transfer.
whyWrong: Meeting one objective doesn't by itself achieve a broad goal, and the rise in complaints suggests service hasn't improved.
The objective was about how quickly calls were answered, and that target was met; complaints are a separate measure.
The software met its target. The evidence points to reviewing the objectives, not to abandoning the system.

stem: Which is an advantage of in-house software development over external development?
options: The organisation gains specialist skills that its own staff do not have
The organisation keeps direct control over the code and who can see its data
The organisation pays a fixed contract price that covers the whole project
The organisation does not need to employ or train any programming staff
explanation: In-house, the organisation's own staff write the code under its own policies, so it decides the priorities, keeps the work and controls who has access to its data.
whyWrong: Gaining skills the organisation lacks is an advantage of external development.
A contract price applies when an external developer is engaged, not when the organisation's own staff build the software.
In-house development requires the organisation to employ and train developers.

stem: The Shire of Redgum Plains, a regional Victorian council with 500 staff, needs a one-off program to analyse drone images of its roads. None of its IT staff has image-processing experience, and the program is needed within four months. Which recommendation is best justified?
options: In-house, because staff know the council's processes and can learn image processing as they build
In-house, because an external developer would become the owner of the council's road data
External, because an external developer is not bound by the council's security requirements
External, because a specialist developer has the skills the council lacks and can meet the deadline
explanation: The council lacks the specialist skills, the program is a one-off and the deadline is short. A specialist external developer suits all three, provided the contract covers security and ownership.
whyWrong: Learning a specialist skill during the project puts the four-month deadline at risk.
Sharing data with a developer doesn't make the developer its owner; the contract sets how it may be used.
The contract should bind the developer to the council's security requirements; ignoring them is no advantage.

stem: Which is the most significant security risk of having software developed externally?
options: The developer's staff may access confidential data under practices the organisation can't control
The organisation's own developers may lack the skills needed to write secure code for the project
The developer may use naming conventions that differ from those in the organisation's other programs
Code written by the developer cannot be checked by the organisation's own code reviews
explanation: External development gives a third party access to the organisation's data and code. The organisation can set contract terms but can't directly control the developer's staff, systems or security practices.
whyWrong: A lack of in-house skills is a risk of in-house development, not external development.
Inconsistent naming makes maintenance harder but isn't a security risk.
The organisation can and should review delivered code; outsourcing doesn't prevent code review.

stem: Cumbungi Grocers, a Shepparton supermarket chain with 1200 staff, has contracted Peppercress Software to build a loyalty app. The app will store customers' names, email addresses and purchase histories. Which contract term best protects Cumbungi Grocers' customer data during development?
options: Peppercress Software pays a penalty for each day the app is delivered after the agreed date
Peppercress Software writes the app in a language that Cumbungi Grocers' developers know
Peppercress Software tests with invented data and limits real customer data to named staff
Peppercress Software hands over the source code and its documentation when the project ends
explanation: Invented test data means real customer details aren't needed for most development, and naming the staff who may access real data limits who could expose it.
whyWrong: A late-delivery penalty protects the schedule, not the customer data.
This helps later maintenance but does nothing to protect data during development.
Handing over the code secures ownership and maintenance after the project, not the data during it.

stem: Wombelano Transport, a Hamilton freight company with 350 staff, paid an external software firm to build a driver-rostering app. When the app was delivered, it rostered drivers in ways that broke the company's own rest-break rules. Every Wombelano Transport manager knows these rules, but no one thought to include them in the requirements. Which disadvantage of external development does this most directly show?
options: The firm's staff may see company data under practices the company can't control
The firm doesn't know the company's processes, so unwritten rules are missed
The company must pay the firm again for each change it needs after delivery
The firm may keep the source code unless the contract says it must be handed over
explanation: An external firm starts without the organisation's knowledge of its own processes and builds what the requirements say. Rules that staff take for granted, like Wombelano Transport's rest-break rules, are easily left out, and the firm has no way of knowing they exist. Developers employed by the company are more likely to know them. The company can reduce this risk by having staff who know its processes check the requirements and test the app before accepting it.
whyWrong: No company data was exposed here; the problem is that the app follows the wrong rules.
Changes may cost extra later, but the scenario shows why the app went wrong: the firm didn't know the rules.
Nothing suggests a dispute over the source code; the app was delivered but follows the wrong rules.

stem: Cinnabar Gully Nurseries, a Monbulk plant wholesaler with 150 staff, had its ordering system built in-house by Dimitri, its only developer. He wrote no documentation, and no one else understands the code. Which risk does this create most directly?
options: If Dimitri leaves, no one may be able to fix or patch the system quickly
Dimitri can't use version control, because no other developer shares the code
Customers' orders will have to be shared with a third-party developer
The nursery will be charged a fee each time the system needs to be changed
explanation: In-house development depends on the organisation's own staff. With one developer and no documentation, everything known about the code sits with Dimitri. If he leaves or is unavailable, faults and security flaws could stay unfixed while someone new learns the code.
whyWrong: Version control works for a single developer too; the problem is that only Dimitri understands the code.
Nothing is shared with a third party, because the system is built and maintained in-house.
Fees for changes are a disadvantage of external development; Dimitri is on staff.

stem: Tuan Creek Hospital, a regional hospital with 900 staff, has engaged four developers from an external firm to rebuild its staff rostering system. They will need access to the hospital's systems for six months. Which arrangement best protects the hospital's systems and data?
options: One shared account for the firm, limited to the test environment and closed at the end
An individual account each, with full access and a confidentiality agreement signed
An individual account each, limited to the test environment and reviewed after the end
An individual account each, limited to the test environment and closed at the end
explanation: Individual accounts mean every action can be traced to one person. Limiting them to the test environment keeps the contractors away from live systems and data the rebuild doesn't need, and closing them when the contract ends removes access as soon as it is no longer required.
whyWrong: A shared account means no action can be traced to one developer, and one person's access can't be removed on its own.
Full access reaches live systems and data the rebuild doesn't need; an agreement doesn't limit what an account can reach.
The accounts would stay open after the work ends, until someone gets round to reviewing them.

stem: Which of the following is a vulnerability rather than a threat?
options: A criminal group that sells stolen customer records online
A disgruntled developer who plans to copy the source code
A storm that cuts power to the building holding the servers
A test server still using the manufacturer's default password
explanation: A vulnerability is a weakness that could be exploited. Default passwords are widely known, so the test server is open to anyone who tries one.
whyWrong: The criminal group is a threat: people who could exploit a weakness.
The disgruntled developer is an insider threat, not a weakness in the system.
The storm is a threat: an event that could cause harm.

stem: Quollstack Games, a Melbourne studio with 90 staff, builds and tests new features directly on the server that runs its live online game. Which risk does this practice create most directly?
options: Developers will be unable to use version control to record their changes
An untested change could crash the live game or expose players' account data
Players' passwords could be intercepted as they travel to the game server
The studio's source code will become the property of the server's hosting company
explanation: Without separate development and testing environments, untested code runs on the live server. A faulty change can take the game down for every player, and developers work alongside real player data.
whyWrong: Version control works wherever the code runs; the problem is where untested code runs.
Interception in transit is a risk of unencrypted connections, not of where developers build and test.
Hosting code on a server doesn't transfer its ownership.

stem: A developer at Mudbrick Logistics accidentally pushed code containing the company's database password to a public online repository. The next day she deleted the password from the code and pushed the change. Why is the database still at risk?
options: The deletion must pass a code review before the repository hides the earlier version
Public repositories are read-only, so the push that removed the password was rejected
Earlier versions still contain the password, and someone may already have copied it
The password was encrypted in the repository, and anyone who copies it can decrypt it
explanation: Version control keeps every earlier version, so the password can still be read from the history, and anyone may have copied it while it was public. The password must be changed, not just deleted from the code.
whyWrong: Code review checks changes before they are merged; it can't hide versions already published.
The owner can push changes to a public repository, so the deletion was recorded.
A password written into code is plain text, not encrypted; the risk is that anyone can read it.

stem: At Tawny Frogmouth Analytics, a Geelong data company with 300 staff, a developer made a cloud storage folder public so that a client could download a test build. The folder also held a database export containing customer records. Which statement best describes this incident?
options: An insider's configuration mistake created a vulnerability that exposed personal data
An external threat exploited an unpatched vulnerability in the cloud storage service
A malicious insider deliberately stole customer records and passed them to the client
A logic error in the test build revealed customer records to the client who ran it
explanation: The developer had legitimate access and made a configuration mistake. The public folder is the vulnerability, and it exposed the customer records, as well as the test build, to anyone who found it.
whyWrong: No outside attacker or unpatched flaw was involved; a staff member made the folder public.
Nothing suggests intent; the developer was trying to share a test build.
The records were exposed by the folder's settings, not by an error in the program's logic.

stem: Mopoke Hill Ticketing, a Melbourne ticketing company with 120 staff, released its new booking website with the developers' detailed error messages still switched on. When a booking fails, the page shows the database's table names, the query that failed and the server's folder structure. Why is this a vulnerability?
options: It shows attackers how the system is built, which helps them plan an attack
It lets customers see other customers' booking details whenever a booking fails
It slows the website down, so customers give up on their bookings before paying
It stops the developers from using version control to roll back the new release
explanation: Detailed error messages help while a program is being developed, but on the live site they reveal how the system is built. Attackers can use table names, queries and folder paths to craft attacks on the database. The live site should show a general message and record the detail where only the developers can see it.
whyWrong: The messages reveal how the system is built, not other customers' booking details.
Error messages don't slow the site, and speed is a performance problem rather than a security weakness.
Error messages have nothing to do with version control, which still records the release and can roll it back.

stem: Hana, a developer at Sheoak Rise Clinics, a Ballarat medical group with 300 staff, copies real patient records onto her work laptop so that she can keep testing at home. The laptop's drive is not encrypted. Which option describes the risk in this situation, rather than a threat, a vulnerability or a control?
options: The laptop isn't encrypted, so anyone who holds it can open the patient files
A thief who breaks into her car and takes the laptop on her way home from work
Laptops are often lost or stolen, and exposed records would do serious harm
Encrypting the laptop's drive so that its files can't be read without the key
explanation: Risk combines how likely harm is with how severe it would be. Laptops are often lost or stolen, so exposure is likely, and patient records are sensitive, so exposure would cause serious harm. Together these make the risk high.
whyWrong: This is the vulnerability: the weakness (an unencrypted laptop) that a threat could exploit.
This is a threat: a person who could exploit the weakness.
This is a control: a measure that would reduce the risk.

stem: An audit of Hooded Plover Studios, a Collingwood game developer with 70 staff, found four weaknesses: every developer has administrator rights to the code repository, code reviews are optional, the office Wi-Fi password is two years old and the repository is backed up weekly. On his last day, a departing developer deleted the project's main repository. Which weakness most directly allowed him to do this?
options: Code reviews are optional, so no one checked his changes first
Every developer holds administrator rights to the repository
The Wi-Fi password is two years old, so many people may know it
The repository is backed up only once a week, not every night
explanation: Deleting a whole repository needs administrator rights. Because every developer holds them, any one of them, including someone about to leave, can delete it. If only one or two trusted staff held these rights, the departing developer couldn't have done it.
whyWrong: Code review checks changes to the code before they are merged; deleting the repository isn't a change that goes through review.
He used his own staff account, so the Wi-Fi password played no part in the deletion.
Weekly backups affect how much work can be recovered, not whether he could delete the repository.

stem: Which of these is a physical security control?
options: A swipe-card lock on the room that holds the development servers
An authenticator app that gives a code each time a developer logs in
Encryption of the database backups that are copied to cloud storage
A rule that a second developer reviews every change before merging
explanation: A swipe-card lock restricts who can physically enter the server room, protecting the hardware itself.
whyWrong: The authenticator app is part of software authentication, even though it runs on a phone.
Encryption is a software control that protects the stored data.
Code review is a check on the code, not a physical barrier.

stem: Which login process uses multi-factor authentication?
options: A password, then an answer to a security question about the user's first school
A password, then a four-digit PIN that the user chose when the account was set up
A fingerprint scan followed by a face scan, both checked against stored biometrics
A password, then a one-time code from an authenticator app on the user's phone
explanation: The password is something the user knows, and the phone running the authenticator app is something they have. Factors from two different categories make it multi-factor.
whyWrong: The password and the security answer are both something you know.
The password and the PIN are both something you know.
A fingerprint and a face are both something you are, so only one category is used.

stem: A developer at Greenhood Software is testing the login function shown, which should lock an account after three failed attempts. Arrays are indexed from 0. What does `checkLogin(["Wombat1", "Kanga!8", "kanga7", "Kanga!7"], "Kanga!7")` return?
options: `"Access granted"`, because the fourth attempt matches the correct password
`"Account locked"`, because the loop stops once `failures` reaches 3
`"Account locked"`, because `failures` reaches 4 before the loop stops
Nothing, because `i` goes past the last index and causes a runtime error
explanation: Attempts 0, 1 and 2 don't match, so `failures` becomes 3 and `i` becomes 3. The condition `failures < 3` is now false, so the loop ends before the fourth attempt is compared and the function returns `"Account locked"`. The lockout works as intended: after three failures even the correct password is refused, which stops an attacker guessing passwords indefinitely.
whyWrong: The fourth attempt is never compared: the loop has already stopped after three failures.
`failures` stops at 3, because the loop condition is checked before each further comparison.
`i` only reaches 3, and `attempts[3]` is never read, so no index goes out of range.

figures.title: Login function
figures.code:
FUNCTION checkLogin(attempts, correct)
    failures ← 0
    i ← 0
    granted ← FALSE
    WHILE granted = FALSE AND failures < 3 DO
        IF attempts[i] = correct THEN
            granted ← TRUE
        ELSE
            failures ← failures + 1
        ENDIF
        i ← i + 1
    ENDWHILE
    IF granted = TRUE THEN
        RETURN "Access granted"
    ELSE
        RETURN "Account locked"
    ENDIF
ENDFUNCTION

stem: Wallaby Grass Software, a Leongatha company with 40 staff, backs up its code repository every night to a removable drive, which is then kept in a locked safe at another site. When ransomware encrypted the repository server, the team found the backup drive couldn't be read: no one had ever tried restoring from it. Which control would most likely have allowed the company to recover its code?
options: Multi-factor authentication for every developer who logs in to the repository
Encryption at rest for the source code stored on the server's drives
Regularly restoring from the backups to check that they actually work
A code review of every change before it is merged into the repository
explanation: The backup was kept off-site, but it had never been tested, so no one knew it couldn't be read. Restoring from the backups regularly shows whether they work while there is still time to fix them, so a usable copy of the code would have been available.
whyWrong: Multi-factor authentication makes unauthorised logins harder but doesn't recover data once it has been encrypted.
Ransomware can encrypt files that are already encrypted, and this does nothing to make the backup readable.
Code review checks changes for flaws; it provides no working copy of the code to restore.

stem: Mitta Flat Software, a Wodonga developer with 60 staff, runs a full set of test cases on every change before it is merged. Which problem is a code review most likely to find that these tests would miss?
options: A discount that is calculated wrongly for orders over $100
A crash that happens when the quantity box is left empty
A total that is displayed with three decimal places, not two
A database password written as plain text in the code
explanation: Tests check what a program does with given inputs. A password written into the code doesn't change any output, so every test still passes, yet anyone who can read the code can use it. A reviewer reading the code will see it.
whyWrong: A wrong discount changes the output, so a test with an order over $100 would reveal it.
A crash on an empty box is found by any test that leaves the box empty.
Wrongly formatted output shows up as a difference between expected and actual output.

stem: Manna Gum Bank, a Shepparton bank with 900 staff, is moving Mei, a developer, from its payments team to the team that maintains its public website. Under identity and access management, what should happen to Mei's access?
options: She keeps her payments access and gains website access, in case she is needed
Her payments access is removed, and she gets only the website access she needs
She is given administrator rights, so that she can help either team if necessary
Her payments access stays until her next annual review, when it is checked again
explanation: Identity and access management updates a person's access whenever they join, change roles or leave. Mei no longer works on the payments systems, so keeping that access adds risk with no benefit: if her account were misused or taken over, it could still reach payment data.
whyWrong: Access kept 'just in case' builds up over time, so a stolen account could reach systems she no longer works on.
Administrator rights give far more access than either role needs, which increases the damage a stolen account could do.
She would keep access she no longer needs for months; access should change as soon as her role does.

stem: Bettong Hill Apps' policy is that a change may be merged into its code only after a developer other than its author has approved it. Before each merge, its repository runs the function shown. Which call returns TRUE although the policy should refuse the merge?
options: `canMerge("Ari", "Bea", TRUE)`
`canMerge("Ari", "", TRUE)`
`canMerge("Ari", "Ari", TRUE)`
`canMerge("Ari", "Bea", FALSE)`
explanation: Line 3 checks only that the change is approved and that a reviewer is named. It never compares the reviewer with the author, so Ari can approve their own change and the merge goes ahead. That defeats the point of a code review, which is a second person checking the code. Adding `AND reviewer ≠ author` to the condition on line 3 fixes it.
whyWrong: Bea, a different developer, approved the change, so the policy allows it and TRUE is correct.
No reviewer is named, so the function returns FALSE, which is what the policy requires.
The change isn't approved, so the function returns FALSE, which is correct.

figures.title: Merge check
figures.code:
FUNCTION canMerge(author, reviewer, approved)
    // Policy: merge only after a developer other than the author approves
    IF approved = TRUE AND reviewer ≠ "" THEN
        RETURN TRUE
    ELSE
        RETURN FALSE
    ENDIF
ENDFUNCTION

stem: What is the main purpose of threat modelling in software development?
options: To test the finished program with real users and record usability problems
To record every change to the source code so that it can be rolled back
To identify threats to a system early and plan controls that mitigate them
To show the project's tasks, their durations and the dependencies between them
explanation: Threat modelling finds what could go wrong with a system's security, ideally during design, so that controls can be planned and built in.
whyWrong: This describes beta testing, which checks a working solution with users rather than its security.
This describes version control.
This describes a Gantt chart, a project management tool.

stem: Tidewater Pharmacy, a Warrnambool pharmacy group with 180 staff, is threat modelling the online ordering system shown in the DFD. The team identifies the threat that an attacker could intercept `payment_details` as they travel over the internet. Which control best mitigates this threat?
options: Encrypt the payment details while they travel to the payment provider
Require customers to use multi-factor authentication when they log in
Back up the Orders data store to an off-site location every night
Have a second developer review the code for the Place order process
explanation: Interception targets data while it moves across a network. Encrypting the flow in transit means that intercepted payment details can't be read.
whyWrong: Multi-factor authentication protects against someone logging in as a customer, not against data being intercepted in transit.
Off-site backups protect the stored orders, not data travelling to the payment provider.
Code review may find flaws in the process, but it doesn't protect data crossing the network.

stem: Candlebark Mutual, a Geelong customer-owned bank, has rated four threats to its new banking app during threat modelling. Based on the ratings in the table, which threat should be mitigated first?
options: T4, because it would cause the most severe harm if it occurred
T2, because it is the threat most likely to occur
T1, because it is the quickest and cheapest to mitigate
T3, because it is both likely to occur and severely harmful
explanation: Risk combines likelihood and impact. T3 is rated high on both, so it carries the greatest risk and should be mitigated first.
whyWrong: T4's impact is high, but its low likelihood gives it a lower risk than T3.
T2 is no more likely than T3, and its impact is lower.
The table rates risk, not the cost of a fix, and T1 is rated low on both likelihood and impact.

figures.title: Threat ratings: Candlebark Mutual banking app

Low
Low

stem: Spadefoot Ticketing's threat model lists the threat that a logged-in customer could change the booking number in a web address to view another customer's booking. The planned mitigation is a check that each requested booking belongs to the logged-in customer. Which activity best confirms that the threat has been mitigated?
options: Confirm that the Gantt chart shows the check was finished before the release milestone
As one test customer, request another test customer's booking and confirm it is refused
Survey customers on whether they feel confident that their bookings are kept private
Check that the code for the check has internal documentation explaining its purpose
explanation: Only a test that attempts the attack shows the mitigation works. If the check was built correctly, a request for another customer's booking is refused.
whyWrong: The Gantt chart shows the task was scheduled or finished, not that the check blocks the threat.
Customers' confidence doesn't show whether the check refuses unauthorised requests.
Documentation explains the code but doesn't prove it blocks the threat.

stem: Dunnart Fitness, a Frankston gym chain with 260 staff, is threat modelling its class-booking app by working through the DFD shown one element at a time. Which threat applies most directly to data store D1, Members?
options: `login_details` are intercepted as they travel to process 1, Log in
An attacker who reaches the database copies the stored member details
Someone poses as Head office to receive the `attendance_summary`
A member books classes in another member's name at process 2, Book class
explanation: A data store holds data at rest, so the threats to it are that the stored data is read, copied, changed or deleted by someone who shouldn't have it. Controls for D1 would include limiting which accounts can read it and encrypting the stored member details.
whyWrong: Interception is a threat to data moving along a flow, `login_details`, not to data held in D1.
This concerns the Head office entity and the `attendance_summary` flow, not the stored member details.
This is a threat to process 2, which records bookings; it doesn't read or change the member records in D1.

stem: The threat model for a Melbourne tutoring company's online lesson portal lists the threat that an attacker could try thousands of passwords against a student's account. Which security requirement best addresses this threat?
options: The portal must be secure and must protect students' personal details
Students must be able to join a booked lesson in three taps or fewer
Lesson records must be backed up to a second site every night
After five failed logins, an account must be locked for 15 minutes
explanation: A security requirement states, in a form that can be tested, what the solution must do to protect its data. Locking an account after five failed logins stops an attacker trying thousands of passwords, and a tester can check it by entering five wrong passwords.
whyWrong: It is too vague to test, and it doesn't say what the portal must do about password guessing.
It is a usability requirement for joining lessons, not a control on password guessing.
Backups help recover lost records, but they do nothing to stop passwords being guessed.

stem: Psyche Bend Accounting, a Mildura firm with 90 staff, develops its own client portal. Its threat model includes the threat that a developer accidentally releases a faulty change that takes the portal offline. Which control reduces the impact of this threat rather than its likelihood?
options: Version control, so the last working version can be restored quickly
A code review by a second developer before every change is merged
Testing each change in a separate test environment before its release
Training every developer in the firm's coding standards once a year
explanation: Likelihood is how probable it is that a faulty change goes live; impact is how much harm it does once it has. Review, separate testing and training all make a faulty release less likely, but none of them helps once one is live. Version control keeps every earlier version, so the team can restore the last working version quickly, which shortens the outage and limits the harm to clients.
whyWrong: Review catches faults before release, so it makes a faulty release less likely; it doesn't shorten an outage.
Testing first catches faults before they go live, which reduces likelihood, not the harm once a fault is live.
Better coding practice means fewer faulty changes, which reduces likelihood rather than impact.

stem: Which of the following is the most suitable criterion for evaluating the security of an organisation's software development practices?
options: The development team says it feels confident about its security
The finished program responds to every request within two seconds
All code repository accounts require multi-factor authentication
The project is completed on time and within its approved budget
explanation: A criterion must be specific and checkable, and it must concern how securely software is developed. Whether every repository account requires multi-factor authentication can be checked against the account settings.
whyWrong: Confidence is an opinion, not evidence, so it can't show whether practices are secure.
Response time measures the solution's performance, not how securely it is developed.
Time and budget judge the project plan, not the security of development practices.

stem: An evaluator reviewed the development practices of Paperbark Insurance, a Geelong insurer, and recorded the findings below. Which criterion does the evidence show is **not** met?
options: Repository accounts are protected by multi-factor authentication
Every change is approved by a second developer before merging
Third-party libraries are patched soon after updates are released
Test environments contain no identifiable customer information
explanation: A nightly full copy of the live customer database puts identifiable personal information in the test environment, so this criterion is not met. The evidence shows that the other three criteria are met.
whyWrong: The evidence shows all 12 developers use multi-factor authentication.
The merge log shows a second developer approved every change.
Patches were applied within a week of release, so this criterion is met.

figures.title: Evaluation findings
rows: Logging in
All 12 developers use multi-factor authentication to reach the repository
Code changes
The merge log shows a second developer approved every change in the last six months
Libraries
Patches for third-party libraries were applied within a week of release
Testing
The test database is refreshed each night with a full copy of the live customer database

stem: Which evidence would best show whether the criterion 'former staff lose access to the code repository on their last day' is met?
options: Departure dates in staff records compared with account closure dates
A survey asking current developers how secure they believe access is
A code review of recent changes checking for hard-coded passwords
A test table comparing expected and actual outputs of the login module
explanation: The criterion is about timing. Comparing when each person left with when their account was closed shows directly whether access was removed on their last day.
whyWrong: A survey collects opinions, which can't show when accounts were actually closed.
A code review checks changes for flaws and secrets, not whether leavers' accounts were closed.
A test table checks that the login module works, not when accounts were closed.

stem: Tern Bay Software in Warrnambool is concerned that an authorised developer could change its live system without approval. Which criterion would best evaluate whether its development practices address this risk?
options: Production databases are encrypted using a strong, managed key
Changes reach production only through an approved, logged release
A full backup of production is taken and stored off-site each day
All developer accounts use multi-factor authentication to log in
explanation: The threat is an authorised insider making unapproved changes. A criterion that every change reaches production only through an approved, logged release checks both that approval happens and that each change can be traced.
whyWrong: Encryption protects stored data from outsiders; an authorised developer can still make changes.
Backups help recovery after a bad change but don't stop unapproved changes being made.
Multi-factor authentication confirms who logs in, but the risk comes from a legitimate, logged-in developer.

stem: Nardoo Payroll Services in Mildura is evaluating its development practices against the criterion 'Access to the live payroll database follows the principle of least privilege.' The evaluator found that all nine developers can change the live database, each through an individual account protected by multi-factor authentication. Only the two developers who carry out releases need that access. Which conclusion does this evidence best support?
options: Not met, because seven developers can change live data they have no need to change
Met, because each developer logs in with an individual account rather than a shared one
Met, because every account that can reach the live database uses multi-factor authentication
Not met, because even the two release developers should have no access to the live database
explanation: Least privilege means each account has only the access its owner's role needs. Seven of the nine developers can change live payroll data without needing to, so the criterion isn't met. Individual accounts and multi-factor authentication are worthwhile, but they are evidence for other criteria.
whyWrong: Individual accounts make actions traceable, but least privilege is about how much access each account has.
Multi-factor authentication confirms who is logging in; it doesn't limit what each account can do.
The two developers who carry out releases need that access for their role, so least privilege allows it.

stem: Glider Gully Games is a four-person Ballarat studio. Its developers work from home on company laptops, and the studio keeps its code in a cloud-hosted repository instead of on a server of its own. Which proposed criterion is **least** relevant to evaluating the security of Glider Gully Games' development practices?
options: Every company laptop has its whole drive encrypted
Every repository account requires multi-factor authentication
Repository access is removed on each person's last day
Entry to the server room is logged by a swipe-card reader
explanation: A useful criterion is linked to a real risk for the organisation being evaluated. Glider Gully Games keeps its code in the cloud and has no server of its own, so there is no server room to protect. A criterion about logging entry to one can't be applied, and it says nothing about how securely the studio develops its code.
whyWrong: Laptops used at home can be lost or stolen, so drive encryption protects the code stored on them.
A cloud repository can be reached from anywhere, so multi-factor authentication is highly relevant.
Former staff could still reach the cloud repository from home, so removing access promptly is relevant.

stem: A Bendigo credit union is evaluating its development practices against the criterion 'No passwords or keys are stored in source code.' Which method of collecting evidence would give the most reliable result?
options: Search the latest version of each file in the repository for passwords and keys
Search every version of each file in the version history for passwords and keys
Ask each developer to confirm in writing that they have never put a password in code
Check the account settings to confirm every repository account uses multi-factor authentication
explanation: Version control keeps every earlier version of each file, so a password removed from the latest code can still be read in the history by anyone with access to the repository. Only a search of the whole history shows whether a password or key is stored anywhere in the source code.
whyWrong: A password deleted from the latest version is still stored in earlier versions, so this search could miss it.
A written statement relies on each developer's memory and honesty; it isn't a check of what the code actually contains.
This is evidence for a different criterion, about logging in, not about secrets stored in code.

stem: Which statement best describes the Essential Eight?
options: Eight privacy principles that Australian Government agencies must follow
Eight mitigation strategies published by the Australian Cyber Security Centre
A Victorian Act setting data security standards for state public sector bodies
An eight-step threat modelling process for designing secure software
explanation: The Essential Eight is a set of eight prioritised strategies from the Australian Cyber Security Centre, such as patching, multi-factor authentication and regular backups, that reduce cyber security risk.
whyWrong: Privacy principles for Australian Government agencies are the Australian Privacy Principles in the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth).
Standards for the Victorian public sector come from the Privacy and Data Protection Act 2014 (Vic), not the Essential Eight.
The Essential Eight lists mitigation strategies; it isn't a threat modelling process.

stem: Wattleglen Physiotherapy, a private clinic in Bendigo, is having an app built that stores each patient's injury history and treatment notes. Which statement about the law that applies to this information is correct?
options: The Privacy and Data Protection Act 2014 (Vic) applies, because the clinic is in Victoria
No privacy law applies, because the clinic is a private business, not a government body
Only the Essential Eight applies, because the information is stored electronically
The Health Records Act 2001 (Vic) applies, because the clinic holds health information
explanation: Injury histories and treatment notes are health information. The Health Records Act 2001 (Vic) regulates how public and private organisations in Victoria handle health information, so the clinic and its app must follow its Health Privacy Principles.
whyWrong: That Act binds Victorian public sector bodies and their contractors, not a private clinic.
Private organisations that hold health information in Victoria are bound by privacy law.
The Essential Eight is guidance, not law, and it doesn't regulate how health information is handled.

stem: Mount Corella Shire Council in regional Victoria is replacing its rates system. The new system will store ratepayers' names, addresses and payment histories. Which Act most directly governs how the council handles this personal information, and why?
options: The Privacy and Data Protection Act 2014 (Vic), as councils are Victorian public sector bodies
The Privacy Act 1988 (Cth), as it covers every organisation that holds personal information
The Health Records Act 2001 (Vic), as payment histories are sensitive personal records
The Copyright Act 1968 (Cth), as the council owns the records stored in its system
explanation: A local council is part of the Victorian public sector, so its handling of personal information is governed by the Privacy and Data Protection Act 2014 (Vic) and its Information Privacy Principles.
whyWrong: The Privacy Act doesn't cover every organisation; it excludes state public sector bodies such as Victorian councils.
Names, addresses and payment histories aren't health information, so the Health Records Act doesn't apply.
Copyright protects works such as program code; it doesn't govern how personal information is handled.

stem: A developer at Mulgara Outdoor Supplies, a Kerang retailer covered by the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth), leaves a customer database publicly accessible. An unknown party downloads customers' names, dates of birth and driver licence numbers, and serious harm to those customers is likely. What does the Act require the retailer to do?
options: Notify the Victorian Information Commissioner, as the retailer is in Victoria
Restore the database from a backup, which ends any duty to notify anyone
Notify the affected customers and the Australian Information Commissioner
Record the breach in its risk register, since notification is optional
explanation: Under the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme, an organisation covered by the Privacy Act must notify the affected individuals and the Australian Information Commissioner (through the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner) of a breach that is likely to cause serious harm, so that people can protect themselves, for example by replacing their driver licence.
whyWrong: The Victorian commissioner oversees the Victorian public sector; a private retailer covered by the Privacy Act notifies the Australian commissioner.
Restoring the data doesn't undo the download; the customers remain at risk and must be told.
Notification isn't optional when a breach is likely to cause serious harm.

stem: At a Swan Hill freight software company, developers can download and run any program on the build server. Last month a developer ran a free code-formatting tool that turned out to contain malware. Which Essential Eight strategy most directly prevents this from happening again?
options: Regular backups, so that the build server can be restored
Patch operating systems, so that the server's known flaws are fixed
Multi-factor authentication, so that every login needs two factors
Application control, so that only approved programs can run
explanation: Application control lets only approved programs run on a computer. An unapproved tool downloaded from the internet would be blocked on the build server, whether or not it contained malware.
whyWrong: Backups help the company recover after malware has run; they don't stop it running.
Patching closes known vulnerabilities, but here a logged-in developer ran the malicious tool themselves.
The developer was legitimately logged in, so a second factor wouldn't have stopped the tool running.

stem: Kooranga Hills Shire Council in regional Victoria runs a maternal and child health service. Its developers are building an app in which the service's nurses record each child's growth, immunisations and health checks. Which Act sets the privacy rules for how the council handles this information in the app?
options: The Privacy and Data Protection Act 2014 (Vic), because the council is a Victorian public sector body
The Health Records Act 2001 (Vic), because the app holds health information about each child
The Privacy Act 1988 (Cth), because it covers health information held anywhere in Australia
The Copyright Act 1968 (Cth), because the council owns the records created in its app
explanation: Growth, immunisation and health check records are health information. The Health Records Act 2001 (Vic) regulates how both public and private sector organisations in Victoria handle health information, so its Health Privacy Principles set the rules for this information. The council's other personal information, such as ratepayers' details, falls under the Privacy and Data Protection Act 2014 (Vic).
whyWrong: That Act's privacy principles cover the council's other personal information, such as ratepayers' details; health information is covered by the Health Records Act instead.
The Privacy Act doesn't cover state public sector bodies, such as Victorian councils.
Copyright protects works such as program code; it doesn't set rules for handling health information.

stem: Which situation raises the ethical issue of failing to acknowledge reused code?
options: A developer writes her own sort function after reading how the algorithm works
A developer calls a library's functions and lists the library in the documentation
A developer reuses a function he wrote last year for the same employer's app
A developer pastes a function from an online forum and comments it as her own work
explanation: Copying a function from a forum and labelling it as her own presents someone else's work as hers and hides where the code came from.
whyWrong: Writing her own code from a description of an algorithm is original work, so there is nothing to acknowledge.
Listing the library in the documentation acknowledges it.
The function is his own work for the same employer, so there is no one else to credit.

stem: Imogen, a junior developer at Quellwood Energy in Ballarat, uses an AI assistant to generate the login module for the customer portal. She commits the code without reading or testing it, because it compiles without errors. Which ethical issue does this most directly raise?
options: Over-reliance on AI-generated code without checking it for flaws
Scope creep from adding features that the client didn't request
Exposure of personal data through an unsecured test environment
Failure to acknowledge a licensed library used in the portal code
explanation: Imogen is trusting AI output she hasn't read or tested. Compiling only shows there are no syntax errors; the module could still contain logic errors or security flaws that expose customers' accounts.
whyWrong: Scope creep is a project management issue, and no extra features are described.
Nothing in the scenario involves a test environment or copied data.
No library is mentioned; the issue is unchecked AI output.

stem: Two days before release, Tomas, a developer at Orchard Lane Payroll in Shepparton, finds a vulnerability that could expose employees' bank details. Which action is the most ethical?
options: Fix it quietly after release, so the client isn't worried by a delay
Report it and its likely impact so a fix or delay can be decided
Add a clause to the terms of use so that users accept the risk
Post details of it online so users can protect themselves now
explanation: Reporting the vulnerability with its likely impact lets the organisation decide, with full information, to fix it or delay the release, which protects the employees whose bank details are at risk.
whyWrong: Releasing with a known flaw and hiding it leaves employees exposed without their knowledge.
Users can't judge a hidden technical risk, so a clause shifts the harm to them rather than preventing it.
Publishing the details before a fix is ready shows attackers how to exploit the flaw, putting employees' bank details at greater risk.

stem: Developers at Tallis Street Insurance in Wodonga copy the live customer database, including names, addresses and bank details, into the test environment because it is quicker than creating test data. Contractors can also reach the test environment. Which statement best explains why this is an ethical issue?
options: Live data lacks the boundary and invalid values that test data needs
The Copyright Act gives each customer ownership of their own records
Customers' data is exposed to more people without their knowledge
Live data makes test results unreliable, so defects reach production
explanation: Customers gave their details to be insured, not to test software. Copying them into a less protected environment that contractors can reach exposes them to more people and more risk, without the customers knowing or agreeing.
whyWrong: Choosing boundary and invalid values is a test data design question, not an ethical one.
Copyright protects works such as code; it doesn't give customers ownership of records about them.
Real data doesn't make results unreliable; the concern is the harm to customers.

stem: Four developers at a Shepparton software company use an AI coding assistant in different ways. Which use shows over-reliance on AI-generated code?
options: Asking it to explain an error message, then writing and testing the fix herself
Accepting its encryption function unread, because it says the code is secure
Having it draft internal documentation, then correcting the draft against the code
Asking it to suggest test data, then checking each value against the requirements
explanation: Accepting code unread, on the assistant's own word that it is secure, hands the developer's judgement to the AI. Encryption code can look correct and still contain flaws that expose data, and the developer, not the assistant, is responsible for the code they commit.
whyWrong: The developer writes and tests the fix herself, so she stays in control of the code.
The draft is checked against the code before it is used, so the AI's output isn't trusted blindly.
Each suggested value is checked against the requirements, so the developer stays responsible for the test data.

stem: Ravi is building a bike-hire app for Moonah Bay Cycle Hire in Inverloch. His manager asks him to make the app record each user's location every five minutes, even when the app is closed, and to leave this out of the app's privacy notice so that the data can be used for marketing later. What is Ravi's most ethical response?
options: Build the feature as asked, because the manager is responsible for the decision
Build the feature, but encrypt the stored locations so the hidden data is safe
Leave the feature out quietly, and tell the manager that it has been built
Explain his concerns, and propose telling users and letting them opt in
explanation: Recording users' locations without telling them takes personal data they haven't agreed to give, for a purpose they don't expect. Raising the concern openly, and proposing that users are told and can choose, respects the users and is honest with his employer.
whyWrong: Ravi shares responsibility for what he builds, and following instructions doesn't remove the harm to users.
Encryption protects the stored data from outsiders, but users still wouldn't know they are being tracked.
Deceiving his manager is dishonest, and the feature could simply be added later by someone else.

stem: Which measure is an example of applying the principle of least privilege?
options: Requiring a password and a code from an authenticator app
Encrypting the customer database with a strong, managed key
Giving software testers read-only access to the test database
Storing a daily copy of the code repository at an off-site location
explanation: Testers need to read test data but not change it, so read-only access gives them only what their role requires.
whyWrong: Requiring two factors is multi-factor authentication, which confirms identity rather than limiting access.
Encryption stops stolen data being read; it doesn't limit each user's access.
An off-site copy is a backup, which supports recovery rather than limiting access.

stem: Lomandra Fitness, a Bairnsdale gym chain, runs a class-booking website built with a third-party library. Eight months ago the library's authors released a new version that fixes a published security flaw, but the website still uses the old version. Which measure most directly reduces the risk from this weakness?
options: Require multi-factor authentication for all developer accounts
Update to the patched version and keep a record of library versions
Encrypt the member database stored on the booking server
Keep a full backup of the booking server at an off-site location
explanation: The flaw has been published, so attackers know what to look for in websites that still run the old version. Updating to the patched version closes the flaw, and a record of the library versions each program uses shows when future updates are needed.
whyWrong: Multi-factor authentication protects developer logins, but attackers can exploit the library's flaw through the website without logging in.
Encryption protects stored data if it is copied, but it leaves the known flaw open to attack.
A backup helps recovery after an attack, but it doesn't close the known flaw.

stem: Karri Lane Pet Supplies stores customers' credit card numbers in its order database. Which measure eliminates, rather than reduces, the risk of those card numbers being exposed if the order database is breached?
options: Encrypting the card numbers with a key stored on a separate server
Requiring multi-factor authentication for database administrators
Reviewing the database access logs for unusual activity each day
Having a payment provider process cards, so none are stored
explanation: If card numbers are never stored in the order database, a breach of that database can't expose them, so the risk is removed rather than lowered.
whyWrong: Encryption reduces the risk, but the numbers are still stored and could be exposed if the key is stolen.
Multi-factor authentication makes unauthorised logins less likely, but the numbers stay in the database.
Monitoring logs helps detect a breach; it doesn't remove the stored numbers.

stem: A consultant proposed the measures below for Lantern Moth Games, a Melbourne game developer. Which pairing of threat and measure is the least effective?
options: Player data copied to USB, met by encrypting data in transit
Phishing of a password, met by multi-factor authentication
A former contractor's login, met by disabling accounts
Ransomware on the file server, met by offline backups
explanation: Encrypting data sent between servers protects it while it travels over a network, but the employee is authorised to see the data and copies it from inside. Least-privilege access to player data and blocking USB storage devices would address this threat.
whyWrong: Multi-factor authentication means a phished password alone isn't enough to log in, so it directly reduces this threat.
Disabling accounts on the last day removes the access the former contractor would use.
Offline backups can't be reached by the ransomware and let the code be restored.

figures.title: Proposed measures
rows: A developer's password is stolen through a phishing email
Require multi-factor authentication for all accounts
A former contractor logs in to the code repository
Disable accounts on each contractor's last day
Ransomware encrypts the source code on the file server
Keep tested backups in an offline location
An employee copies player data to a personal USB drive
Encrypt data sent between the game servers

stem: A Gippsland tour company's booking website connects to its database through an account with full administrator rights. An attacker who took control of the website could therefore delete any table or read the staff records stored in the same database. Which change would most directly limit what such an attacker could do to the database?
options: Give the administrator account a longer and more complex password
Let the website's account only read tour times and handle bookings
Encrypt the connection between the website and the database server
Back up the database every night so that deleted tables can be restored
explanation: This applies the principle of least privilege, which covers programs as well as people: the website's database account gets only the access the website needs. If it can only read tour times and handle bookings, an attacker who takes control of the website can't delete tables or read staff records through it. The other changes leave the account's full rights in place.
whyWrong: A stronger password makes the account harder to guess, but an attacker who controls the website still gets its full rights.
Encrypting the connection protects data in transit; the website's account could still delete tables.
Backups let deleted tables be restored, but the attacker could still delete them and read the staff records.

stem: The five developers at a Wangaratta company that builds stock-control software all log in to the code repository with one shared administrator account. When a change broke the stock count calculation last month, no one could tell who had made it. Which measure would let the company trace each future change to the developer who made it?
options: Add multi-factor authentication to the shared administrator account
Encrypt the repository so the code can't be read if it is copied
Back up the repository every night so earlier versions can be restored
Give each developer their own account with only the rights they need
explanation: Version control records the account that made each change. With one account per developer, every change can be traced to one person, and giving each account only the rights its owner needs also limits the damage any one account can do.
whyWrong: Multi-factor authentication makes the login harder to steal, but all five developers would still share it, so their changes couldn't be told apart.
Encryption protects the code if it is copied; it doesn't record who changed it.
Backups let a broken version be replaced, but they don't show who made the change.

stem: Which of the following is a recommendation rather than a finding?
options: Require a second developer to approve each change before it is merged
Three developers hold administrator rights they don't need for their work
The repository contains a database password written into the source code
The test server's operating system hasn't been updated since March
explanation: A recommendation states an action to take. Requiring approval before merging is an action; the other options describe weaknesses that have been found.
whyWrong: This describes a weakness that was found (unneeded privileges); it doesn't say what to do.
This describes a weakness that was found (a hard-coded password), not an action to take.
This is a finding about missing updates, not a recommended action.

stem: At Numbat Park Studios, a Geelong app developer, the four developers email zipped copies of the source code to each other. Changes are often overwritten, and no one can tell who changed what. Which recommendation best addresses this?
options: Encrypt every email that contains a copy of the source code
Back up each developer's laptop to an external drive every week
Adopt version control, with each developer using their own account
Require comments that state the purpose of every module in the code
explanation: Version control keeps one shared copy of the code with a history of every change, recorded against the account that made it, so overwritten work can be recovered and changes can be traced.
whyWrong: Encryption protects the code in transit, but changes would still be overwritten and untraceable.
Weekly backups keep old copies, but they don't show who changed what or stop overwriting.
Internal documentation explains the code; it doesn't track changes or stop overwriting.

stem: Corvid Lane Media, a three-person Castlemaine web studio with a small budget, found that an attacker had logged in to its cloud code repository using a developer's password leaked from another website. The repository offers multi-factor authentication at no extra cost, but it is switched off. Which recommendation is best justified?
options: Hire a security firm to monitor the repository around the clock
Turn on multi-factor authentication for every repository account
Move the repository to a server in a locked room at the studio
Require developers to change their passwords every two weeks
explanation: The attacker used a valid stolen password. With multi-factor authentication a password alone is no longer enough to log in, so it directly addresses the weakness, and it costs the small studio nothing to turn on.
whyWrong: Round-the-clock monitoring may detect attacks, but it is costly for a three-person studio and doesn't stop a stolen password working.
Moving the server costs money and adds new risks, and a stolen password could still be used to log in.
A password leaked today still works until the next change, and frequent changes encourage weak passwords.

stem: A consultant's report on a development team's practices ends with the recommendation 'Improve security.' Why is this a weak recommendation?
options: It should be written as a non-functional requirement in the SRS
It should name the Act that requires the organisation to improve
It should be phrased as an evaluation criterion, not as an action
It doesn't state a specific action or the risk that it would reduce
explanation: A recommendation must say what to do and why. 'Improve security' names no action, no practice and no risk, so the organisation can't act on it or check whether it worked.
whyWrong: Non-functional requirements describe qualities of a planned solution; this is advice about existing practices.
Not every recommendation needs to cite legislation; the problem is that no action is stated.
Criteria are used to judge practices; a recommendation should be an action.

stem: An evaluation at Striped Gum Media, a Bright video production company, found that a developer's laptop had been infected with malware. The malware used a flaw that an update released two months earlier had fixed, but the developer had switched off automatic updates because they restarted her laptop during work. Which recommendation best addresses the cause of this incident?
options: Restore the developer's laptop from last week's backup, then carry on as before
Send all staff a reminder that switching off automatic updates is a security risk
Manage updates centrally so they install out of hours and can't be switched off
Require multi-factor authentication each time a developer logs in to a laptop
explanation: The cause was that updates restarted laptops during work, so the developer switched them off and a known flaw stayed open. Installing updates out of hours removes the reason to switch them off, and managing them centrally stops them being switched off, so the laptops stay patched.
whyWrong: Restoring the laptop deals with this infection, but updates could be switched off again, leaving the same kind of flaw open.
A reminder doesn't remove the reason she switched updates off, so staff are likely to do it again.
Multi-factor authentication confirms who logs in; it doesn't close the flaw the malware used.

stem: A Mornington real estate agency stores tenants' rental applications, including copies of their driver licences. An evaluation found that the live database password is written in the source code, which all 12 of the agency's contract developers can read. Lucas, the evaluator, recommends moving the password into a protected secrets store and changing it. Which justification best supports his recommendation?
options: Any contractor could use it to read or change the tenants' driver licence copies
Keeping passwords out of source code is widely recommended as good security practice
Moving the password is a small task that a developer could finish within a single day
The password is written in source code that all 12 contract developers can read
explanation: A justification links the recommendation to the risk in the scenario. Anyone who can read the source code can use the password to reach the live database, so moving it out of the code and changing it stops 12 contractors, and anyone who steals their access, from reaching tenants' licence copies.
whyWrong: This is true of any organisation, so it doesn't link the recommendation to the agency's risk.
Being quick shows the recommendation is realistic, but it doesn't say which risk it reduces.
This restates the finding; it doesn't say why the change is needed.

stem: An evaluation of a Traralgon energy retailer's development practices produced the findings shown. Which recommendation should the retailer act on first?
options: Change the test database's default password and block access from the internet
Test a restore from the live database's backups, and then repeat the test regularly
Set developers' laptops to lock automatically after five minutes without use
Change the live database's default password and block access from the internet
explanation: Default administrator passwords are widely known, and anyone on the internet can try them, so an attack on either database is highly likely. Only the live database holds real customers' bank account details, so the impact of an attack on it is by far the highest. The retailer should secure the live database first.
whyWrong: An attack on the test database is just as likely, but it holds only made-up records, so the impact is far lower.
Untested backups matter for recovery after an incident, but they don't make an attack any more likely.
Misusing an unlocked laptop needs someone at it in person within 30 minutes, so it is far less likely than an attack over the internet.

figures.title: Evaluation findings
rows: The test database holds made-up customer records. It can be reached from the internet and still uses the default administrator password it was installed with.
Backups of the live database are kept in a locked safe, but no restore has been tested for a year.
Developers' laptops lock automatically after 30 minutes without use.
The live database holds customers' names, addresses and bank account details. It can be reached from the internet and still uses the default administrator password it was installed with.
